opus-5.5.text:
So the core idea was that we wanted to see how far you could get with a really small amount of data, and if you're only going to use about a thousand examples, every single one has to earn its place. We started from a much bigger pool, around fifty-nine thousand questions, pulled from a bunch of sources: competition math, olympiad-style problems, some science questions, and some quantitative reasoning sets we put together ourselves, like probability questions from PhD qualifying exams and brain-teaser-style problems. Then we filtered that down using three criteria: quality, difficulty, and diversity.

Quality was the most basic one. We threw out anything with formatting problems, broken text, or errors when we tried to generate reasoning traces for it. That's just hygiene.

Difficulty was more interesting. We wanted problems that actually require extended reasoning, because the whole point is to teach the model to think longer. So we took a couple of reasonably strong models, and if they could already solve a question easily, we dropped it. We also used the length of the reasoning trace as a proxy, since longer traces tend to mean harder problems.

Then diversity. If you only filter for difficulty, you end up with a narrow slice, like lots of hard geometry and not much else. So we classified the questions into subject areas, roughly following the Mathematics Subject Classification, and sampled across those domains, while still favoring the longer, harder examples within each one.

What really surprised us was in the ablations: if you pick a thousand examples using just one of those criteria, or pick randomly, you do noticeably worse. And if you train on the full fifty-nine thousand, you barely gain anything over the curated thousand, despite spending far more compute. So the combination of all three is what made such a small dataset work.

r001.rationale: It says problems that reasonably strong models could already solve easily were dropped, so difficulty selection used prior models’ failure to solve as a signal.

r002.rationale: The response describes favoring hard problems and longer reasoning traces, but does not state that selection favored problems with evidence they were solvable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the whole premise of s1 was that you shouldn't need a lot of data to get strong reasoning, so the selection process really mattered. We started by just collecting as much as we could, around 59,000 questions from a bunch of sources: math competitions like AIME and Olympiad problems, things from the standardized test-style datasets, some science questions, PhD-level stuff, and so on. Then we generated reasoning traces and answers for all of them with Gemini's thinking model, so we had a big pool to filter down from.

And then we had three criteria that we used to filter. The first one is just quality. So we removed anything where the API call failed, where formatting was broken, where the trace looked messy. That's pretty basic, but it gets rid of a lot of noise.

The second one is difficulty, and this one is probably the most important. Our intuition was that if a problem is easy, the model already knows how to do it, so there's not much to learn from it. So we took two Qwen models, a 7B and a 32B, and ran them on every question, and if either of them could solve it, we threw the question out. That left us with questions where even a fairly capable model fails. We also used the length of the reasoning trace as a proxy for difficulty, because harder problems tend to require longer thinking.

And the third criterion is diversity. We didn't want a dataset that was all competition math. So we classified each question into a domain, using the Mathematics Subject Classification as a basis, and then sampled across those domains, with a preference for the ones with longer reasoning traces. That got us to 1,000 samples covering around 50 different domains.

What's nice is we did ablations on each of these. If you just pick 1,000 random samples, or only pick for diversity, or only pick for difficulty, you do noticeably worse. And if you train on the full 59K, you actually only get a marginal improvement over the 1,000, at way more compute. So the combination of difficulty, diversity, and quality was really doing the work.

r001.rationale: The response says it used two Qwen models and discarded any question either model could solve, retaining problems that capable models failed.

r002.rationale: The response says Gemini generated traces and answers for all questions, then filters for trace quality. It does not clearly state that selection favored problems based on evidence that they were solvable.

astra-6.text:
We focused on three things: quality, difficulty, and diversity. We wanted problems with reliable answers and good reasoning traces, but we also wanted problems that were challenging enough that the model would actually learn something from them. If it could already solve a question easily, that question was less useful.

Then diversity mattered because we didn’t want a thousand variations of the same math problem. We wanted coverage across different topics and different kinds of reasoning. So we started with a much larger pool and filtered and sampled it down to a thousand examples using those criteria.

The idea wasn’t to capture everything the model needed to know in those thousand examples. It already had a lot of knowledge from pretraining. We were trying to select examples that would help it use that knowledge through a more deliberate reasoning process.

r001.rationale: The response says problems the model could already solve easily were less useful, but does not identify failure by previous models as the difficulty proxy.

r002.rationale: It says the selected problems should have reliable answers and good reasoning traces, communicating evidence that they were solvable.

sol-6.1.text: We focused on three things: quality, difficulty, and diversity. We wanted problems with reliable answers and good reasoning traces, problems that were challenging enough to teach the model something, and a mix of topics so it wouldn’t just learn one narrow type of problem. The idea wasn’t to collect as much data as possible. It was to see how far we could get with a small, carefully selected set—just 1,000 examples.
